I am one of those people who hated Sims 3 and didn't play it for long, so I was reluctant to try Sims 4, especially at such a high price. After reading good player reviews from people who loved Sims 2 as much as I do, I decided to give it a chance, and after playing it a couple of days, I like it a lot.    CONS:  The camera is hard to control.  You can set it to use Sims 3 controls, which helps a little. I'm getting used to it but it should be better.    Interiors of houses are far too dark. I solved this by putting three lights in each room instead of one.    Lots are surprisingly small. I am not a builder, but I know this is disappointing for builders and I hope bigger lots will be available eventually.    There are hardly any service Sims. I want firefighters to put out fires and cops to catch burglars (who aren't in the game right now, either). There is a system to hire town residents to do certain things, but it seems wonky. The caterer at my Sim wedding served food but did not provide a wedding cake. Shouldn't she have?    Teens, young adults, and adults look alike and are the same height. I actually can identify teens by sight so far (not sure why, maybe they have a slighter build), but young adults and adults appear identical and seem to play identically, which makes me wonder why young adults are in the game at all (there's no university yet).  The young adult lifespan seems too long relative to the adult lifespan. This could be corrected by adding a middle-age life stage-- or even changing adult to middle age?    Hardly any places to visit. No restaurants, for example. I am sure venues will be added later.    Furniture choices so far are bland.    CHANGES I DON'T MIND TOO MUCH:  I don't mind the lack of an open world since I am a fan of Sims 2, which doesn't have it. And in Sims 4 you CAN follow your Sim around the neighborhood -- jogging, for instance -- and stop to chat with passers-by. This is nice.    It's too bad toddlers didn't make it into the game.They were very cute and well done in Sims 2, but that life stage had little real impact on the game. If it's brought back in Sims 4 I'd like it to be meaningful. Maybe well-brought up toddlers get an extra trait -- that would make it worth the effort in gameplay terms.    Pools - a weird omission given how iconic it is to drown Sims, but I never drowned any so I can do without pools for now.    Sims 3 players complain about the loading screens in Sims 4, but they are quick and don't bother me.    You have to fix items yourself or replace them, no repairman. This sounds bad but I'm kind of liking it because it adds to the challenge of gameplay. My Sims are trying to save money to move so they fix everything. As they improve in repair ability, they can upgrade appliances so they break less often. I find this interesting, but repairmen should still be an option.    Many items can't be purchased till they're unlocked via career promotions. Again, I like this because it makes the game more challenging.    PROS:  All new animations. When I played Sims 3 I saw the same animations as Sims 2, but in Sims 4 everything I see is new, which makes it fun to watch. It should be that way in every new Sims game.    No rabbit holes, yay! If my Sim is going into a building, I want to go in too, not sit staring at the exterior of the building as in Sims 3.    The multitasking is just as great as everyone says -- Sims can watch TV, eat, and hold a conversation at the same time. In game play this is a lot cooler than it sounds, quite realistic and a big time saver.    I also like the emotions system. It is easily managed if you want to play that way but also adds to unpredictability if you like to be surprised. One of my Sims almost had his wedding ruined when he lost his temper at a quarrelsome guest! I managed to cheer him up before he said his vows. It's nice to know that every party or event won't play out the same way every time.    Walk styles -- yes, they are goofy, but they fitinto the whimsy of the Sim world, and also they help differentiate Sims from each other. I'm glad the Sims series still has a sense of humor.    So far I've had only one minor bug and no crashes. The game runs smoothly. Quite different from the Sims 3 base game, which crashed so much that I was afraid it would damage my computer.    Little touches mean a lot. When the Sims play \\"Sims Forever\\" on their computers, it looks like The Sims 1. That was fun to see. The TV shows are well done, too. Attention to detail shows that someone in charge of creating this game still cares about it.    When I first began playing Sims 4 I wasn't sure how I felt about it, but it grew on me over a couple of days. When I started laughing in pleasant surprise at things that were happening in the game, I knew it had won me over. I still think it costs too much -- EA admits this is a \\"base game,\\" and since it's not a full game I believe it shouldn't be so pricy. But I'm not sorry I bought it. I am having fun and I feel the Sims series is making a comeback with Sims 4. Thank goodness.

review_headline: The game is absolutely beautiful to look at
review_body: 1 star removed because the fighting mechanics are a bit rough on the edges and damage stats on enemies is overbearing even in easiest setting.  The game is absolutely beautiful to look at. The quests are high on dialogue to such an extent that its a bit like playin a movie. This is not everybody's cup of tea, but you can bypass long winded dialogue sequences if you prefer to do things. But by doing that, of course, you will miss out on some character relations and story depth.  Some dialogue options will have an effect on the world as a whole. Help someone and later on they will be friendly. Mow them down or be rude and they might not let you get into a place you need to be without a fight. That's pretty cool.  The crafting/alchemy/gear interface and management is awful. It's totally overwhelming and a lot of the buffs have so little effect it's not really worth dealing with. Some other buffs are well worth doing. But you will be hard pressed to figure it out without consulting the Internet.  Initially, fighting is going to be a real challenge. Like Bloodborne, this game does not forgive and forget damage taken. You get bit hard by an enemy, you're going to have to love with it throughout the fight.  At later levels you're going to be okay. But it is still challenging at hard levels. Of course there are ways to abuse the system and create powers and gear that is going to make any boss fight a piece of cake.  Pros: Beautiful visuals Very European Middle Ages look Lots of deep quests Challenging boss fights  Cons: Serious scripting issues that cause totally unfair damage in battles Hard to control battle dynamics. You press dodge but it will stay on attach until that animation has finished. Needs some more fine tuning. Way too many alchemy an gear/magic components Terribly confusing UI for gear and alexhmy etc.

A very nice blend of RTS, RPG and economic game. You are the ruler of Ardania, Fantasy Kingdom. You construct the guilds, economic buildings, research better weapons and shields. There is a variety of missions and quests, some of which require attacking specific places or killing a monster which requires certain strategy. Others require simultaneous construction of some temples or defending a merchant caravan.

"Majesty 2" has nice, colorful 3D fantasy graphics and music which sets the mood really nice (with some beautifully epic pieces for final monster fights). There is a huge choice of hero classes like warriors, wizards, rogues, clerics, paladins and nice selection of monsters with their dwellings including vampire crypts, elemental portals and wolf dens.

The game has a unique style merging some qualities of "Heroes of Might and Magic", some of "Age of Empires" and others from RPG games. Many missions are really demanding. review_headline: A little rough around the edges but fun!
review_body:
Thank you Aterdux Entertainment for sending us a review code for this game!

In May of 2012 Legends of Eisenwald was successfully funded on Kickstarter with nearly $84,000 raised. Since its funding, it has been beta tested by the backers and greenlit on Steam. Nearly three years later it's now available for everyone to enjoy. Gamers who like 3D RPG tactical strategy games like King's Bounty will find much to like in this title.

Legends of Eisenwald begins with a choice of a character to play. There's a slightly different story for a sword wielding knight, a cunning baroness that is good with a bow, or a mystic who is an expert in alchemy. The mystic is the hardest class to play and is recommended for seasoned gamers.

No matter what class you play, you will be at a disadvantage in each of the eight chapters in this game. You'll only have a couple of soldiers, if any, at the beginning of each chapter. Most of the inventory gets reset too. The number of soldiers in your army maxes out at twelve, but in order to have that many soldiers, you need to have a couple of castles under your control. Before you can besiege a castle, you'll need to have a decent army at your command.

Most towns have villagers willing to join your cause for a meager fee. They're inexperienced, but trainable to become powerful knights and archers. Healers and priests can be hired at Christian churches and pagan temples. If you have money to spare, experienced mercenaries can be hired for a daily fee at taverns and mercenary camps.

Money in this game can be earned by completing side quests, collecting taxes from property under your control, or defeating and looting the local enemy armies. Each area has its own local lore and rumors that can be learned by stopping at taverns and talking to people. Many treasures are waiting to be claimed by brave soldiers willing to search for them. They are often guarded by protective spirits though.

The battles are turn based and the units are placed in hexagons and can attack nearby opponents if they are melee fighters or longer ranged if using archery or magic-based attacks. The battles can be fought manually or auto-resolved if you're in a hurry or lazy like me. Armies with undead spirits need to be defeated by magic users who can harm them since physical attacks against them are useless.

Many, but not all of the side quests have unlockable Steam achievements for completing them. There are other Steam benefits including cloud saves, trading cards, and Steam workshop contributions. Not all of the contributions are fully translated into English though.

The development team, Aterdux, is located in Belarus and I have noticed that some of the text was still in Russian. Some of the dialogue boxes, especially during a gambling card game, were completely blank. Unfortunately, there isn't any voice acting so text is crucial to understanding what is going on. The background music is top notch and worth the extra money for the soundtrack and art book.

Graphically, Legends of Eisenwald is very pretty. The characters and army units are nicely detailed, but are noticeably recycled throughout the game. I was taken aback when I was conversing with a female thief who was identical to a castle baroness I was talking with a few minutes prior. At the very least they should be wearing different clothes!

There's a wide variety of terrain and your army will often stay on the paths, but there are many instances where you'll have to stay off of them. When walking around mountains and forests, the cross-able terrain is not very obvious. To make matters worse, there are some quests that require traveling to a specific pixel in order to progress. These quests can be frustrating, but fortunately they are few and far between the in-depth story arcs.

The lore in the game is well written and it's fun to gain power throughout the land while fleeing from enemies who can easily defeat you. Alliances will be made and broken and there are multiple paths available to achieve the same goal. The Catholic church has a lot of power in this game and I often visited their chapels for healing my wounded army units.

Sadly, the Catholic church is depicted as greedy and power hungry. Other religions including pagans and devil worshipers are also represented and required to interact with to progress the story. Since there are battles with the undead, violence is a given and necromancy is unavoidable.

Taverns are the place to go for alcohol and rumors. Some of the rumors discuss incestuous relationships and other adult situations. Last but not least, there is some language and blasphemy. While Legends of Eisenwald hasn't been rated by ESRB, I would only recommend it teens or older.
Despite the rough edges and objectionable content, Legends of Eisenwald is a great game that mature gamers should look into if they like tactical role playing games. The entry fee of $29.99 is reasonable considering that there is fifty plus hours of gameplay to enjoy. Those who have pre-ordered or kickstarted the game, not only got it for a better price, they were also given a free copy of Discord Times which was the developer's first game. review_headline: A Pretty Good Game Overall — But Also Disappointing in Many Respects
review_body: In my opinion, most of the gushing, rave reviews I have read thus far for Pillars of Eternity are over-rating the game in terms of what the average RPG gamer is looking for or would actually enjoy playing. Pillars of Eternity is a great game for certain niche players, but for the rest of us, well, be forewarned. As far as I can tell, most of the glowing reviews have been written by players who fall squarely and comfortably within that niche.  Be aware, then, that the very reasons I was not that impressed with Pillars may be precisely why you will love it. Still, I think there is value in reading dissenting opinions, if only to learn what some players disliked about this game.  Pillars of Eternity is ideally suited to gamers who are very VERY particular about details, stats, and micromanaging combat and gear. That's not a bad thing, but Pillars' nitpickety-ness began to wear on me pretty quickly. I think it's probably a fair test that if you loved the Baldur's Gate games and are looking for something *exactly* like that sort of experience, then I think you are probably going to love Pillars of Eternity. I felt that Baldur's Gate had a pretty good story, but I would not want to return to that type of game structure again. It's high time time to move on. Pillars, unfortunately, really has not moved on.  My biggest frustrations with Pillars of Eternity were:  -- Tedious and slow travel. Waiting (and waiting … and waiting) for my little troupe of characters to run across maps – even at accelerated speeds (which was at least comical to watch) – became really frustrating. And the loading screens, sheesh. Need to go to upstairs in Building A in Town C? You have my sincere condolences. Brace yourself for an endless succession of loading screens in this game: between zones, entering buildings, going up or downstairs.... Heaven help you if get all the way from Point A to Point F only to learn you really should have spoken with NPC Z back at Point A. Ugh.   -- Slow, clunky combat (micro)management. If you love pause-and-play combat, this game will suit you. As for me, I would have preferred better game AI that allowed me to focus on playing my main character rather than micromanaging multiple characters in my party through each and every encounter, wherein battles can progress with excruciating slowness, as you slowly – oh so slowly – whittle away at your opponents. It's like watching paint dry. As far as what's actually going on -- who knows. All you will see is a confused, writhing muddle of friends and foes and green and red dots, wherein you try to destroy the red dots with whatever green dots you have left.  -- Overlong walls of text. I quickly started tabbing through the multitudinous decision/dialog trees and walls (and I do mean WALLS and WALLS) of text. The story here was just not engaging enough for me to spend that much time reading rather than playing, and the added "bonus" of being able to read the souls of random NPC characters lost me early on, since this ability seemed to add little to nothing of relevance to the main story arc (which itself was a fairly standard snooze-fest, in my opinion). Why should I care what random bystander X, Y, or Z is thinking or has done? Reading these various NPC backstories seemed pointless and uninteresting.  -- Obscure, convoluted, unclear quests. Get ready to spend a lot of time searching the web and wiki sites trying to figure out where to go, whom to speak to, where a particular person might be located, or what to do for the various quests in Pillars of Eternity. This game includes some of the most text-heavy, complicated, wordy, and unclear quests I've encountered in quite some time in any game. I do not mind encountering a puzzle now and then, but this game treats virtually every quest as a puzzle. Again, as I've said repeatedly, this may be exactly what you are looking for … one person's food is another person's poison, so they say.  In short, I wish Pillars of Eternity had been a little more "actiony" like Dungeon Siege or Guild Wars and a little less "stat/micro-managey"  – or at least had offered an option to play the game in a more action-oriented way – for those of us who might want to fight and explore this story and world rather than trudge slowly forward, "min/max/hyper-managing" our way through every blessed inch of the journey.  I guess I was hoping Pillars of Eternity would be more Diablo-like, only with larger NPC parties and a richer story and world, and less … what? "Tedious", I guess, is the word I'm looking for here.  Pillars of Eternity is a fair to good game (hence, the three stars I gave it), but it is not as much fun as I had hoped it would be.

Sniping is always great fun so any game that offers plenty of it has to be a good thing. The sniping in SNIPER ELITE V2 is (as I understand it) pretty realistic. It includes all the conditions that would effect such a task in the real world, including bullet drop, wind speed and direction, body movement etc. There’s no denying the satisfaction when you score a hit, especially a headshot, and this is often augmented by the enjoyable spectacle of the bullet flying through the air in slow-motion towards its target. Personally, I could have lived without the kill-cam’s depiction of the victim’s injuries, but this is only a game so let’s not get too wrapped up in the ethics. Less successful is the close-quarter combat that you are sometimes forced into. The cover-based stealth system is less sophisticated than in some games (Deus Ex: Human Revolution, for example) and aiming at close range can be problematic. This, coupled with a ridiculously keen-eyed AI, can prove frustrating. The graphics are good to very good, with the ruins of a war-torn Berlin particularly well depicted. The story is rather fractured due to the mission-based gameplay but SEV2 isn’t really about story, its about honing your long-range shooting skills, and this it does well.

review_headline: 18 hours in (update beat the game and replaying)
review_body: Update: Bump to 5 stars (and this is why) I have been through the main story line and a ton of side quests now. I am about half way through the main story line a second time now but putting in a lot more time with the side quests this time around. To get the real feel for the game you have to play on the hardest setting. Let me tell you why.  You can play the game on easy but you don't have to try much at all and you feel like your just watching things happen. When you put the game on hard you have to work for everything. You have to learn the fighting engine you have to learn how to use blade oil and potions, to win. You have to "REALLY" play the game.  First thoughts: I pre-ordered this game from PSN as soon as it was able to be ordered. The game released at midnight but it took one hour to download so I was unhappy with that to start but this has no reflection on the game it's self. I have logged 18 hours as of now. I expected a lot from this game, even used a vacation day to be able to play all night.  Graphics: The game graphics are good, I am not going to call them amazing because they are not. If you played the previous Witcher you will see a world of difference but this is a "Big name" game and the graphics are just slightly better than Skyrim (last gen game). 8 out of 10  Controls: When you start the game the controls feel clunky, you get a little nerd eye candy right away to keep you from thinking to much about the controls. Then right away you can run through the controls and get a better picture of what you will be doing. The movements are not real complex but you have get used to them. 8 out of 10  Game play: Game play does not get boring because you always have something to kill be that monsters, humans, dogs, wolves always something. You can always find some small puzzle or new location to check out and that keeps you interested. 7 of 10  Leveling: I hate the leveling system, just wanted to get that out there right away. The leveling system is beyond slow, I am killing everything is sight and my level is just not moving. This makes the game suck at times because when you need better gear to beat something you have to leave the battle and find other stuff to do until you hit a level where you can upgrade to new gear and then go back to the battle you really want to fight (this can take hours). The crafting system is better than the last Witcher but still not great. I do not like much of anything about the inventory/crafting system. 6 of 10  I will add to this review as I play over the next few days.  I am about to beat the main story at this point:  This game is a really solid game. I am sticking with my 4 stars because of a few things I was not thrilled with but as I said it is a solid 4 stars.

product_title: Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn
review_body:
Gameplay is very repetitive and boring. Far too easy to hit max level without understanding job responsibilities. Beautiful environments and detailing. Game music is well done but homogeneous, at times.

FFXIV is more of a copy-cat than a leader in the MMORPG space. I am a long time player of FFXI and many free-to-play MMOs so perhaps my perception of this game is not consistent with opinions of players new to MMORPGs.

Community features are killed by FATEs and Level Sync:
FFXIV's treatment of open-world battles (FATEs) give little no to reason to chat and work together. As the main mechanism for level progression, after the main story-line, FATEs train players to be selfish. Essentially, as long as a large number of individuals participate, you have little chance of losing battles thus you are rewarded for not working together. You can even secure highest reward without remaining through the whole FATE. A major minus because if you don't know how this works you can get left behind to get slaughtered!

Level Sync system needs rework. There is no way for two players (say level 15 and level 10) to grind together at the minimum level 10. Friends have no reason to help you level up as neither player will receive exp so long as Level Sync is not in effect. Level Sync works well in dungeons and FATEs but is non-existent in regular party play.

FFXIV is okay and is early in life-cycle but has fundamental flaws which are based upon stolen ideas which were not great to begin with. FFXIV was designed to secure favor of experienced MMO players (also FFXIV 1.0 veterans) and perhaps suffers lack of identity and cohesion to long-time fans of the Final Fantasy series. I make this point because FFXIV borrows heavily from FFXI and FFXII in terms of structure and visual style but those relationships are severed pretty quickly.

review_headline: Fun, but just not quite there.
review_body:
There are a lot of great in-depth reviews on here, so I'll just add my two cents by saying that the game has a lot of really great potential (it's fun, very creative/unique, dark without being too scary, and an enjoyable time killer) but there are a lot of aspects of the game that are incredibly frustrating and the game would be a lot more enjoyable if they were fixed. For example, on several obstacles I died and was forced to restart at the beginning of a section, not because of any fault of my own but because, thanks to a glitch, Alice randomly decided to run without me even pushing the button, and there was absolutely NO WAY to get her to stop. Thanks to another glitch, in which you get stuck with your ranged weapon ONLY, I had to exit and reopen the game at least 10x. Thankfully others had had the same issue and discovered a way to fix it (most of the time).

The save points are an incredibly frustrating aspect as well, it would be fine if there was a manual option in addition to the autosave, but there isn't. So, if you want to save your progress, you have to keep playing the game until you get the little save icon or do it all over again next time you play the game. This is particularly frustrating when you FINALLY beat that enemy or get past that obstacle and are ready for a break, but you have to keep playing for another 30 minutes just to save your progress. And if you die between now and then you're SOL and get to do it all over again anyways! God forbid you're in a rush... Definitely not a game I can play before work or anything. Thanks to the save locations I was also forced to repeat several areas (ex: one save point is up on a ledge, behind you is a Memory. But even if you got the Memory before it saved, you still have to run back and get it anyways when you play the game the next time). It's also frustrating to finally beat an obstacle and head on to the next only to die and have to repeat all the obstacles all over again (sometimes several times in a row, if you happen to get a long line of tough ones).

Is it fun? Definitely! Will I keep playing it? ... Probably, with LOOONG breaks when I'm too ticked to think straight. Will I play it again after I beat it 100%? Probably not. Would I recommend it to a friend? Probably not, and especially not without warning them of the many glitches and problems with the game. I think it has a lot of potential, and I will definitely be interested in Alice 3 when/if it comes out, but this game feels very unfinished in terms of playability. review_headline: Most fun Ever in an MMO / RPG game - Update
review_body: Update - Nov 2014. Still having so much fun playing!  I now have a Rogue, a Mage, and a Paladin. One in each Faction so I am seeing all of Tamriel. The bank is common to all your characters (each character can access the same bank slots).  There are hardly any bots or bugs left in the game as far as I can see. Combat - you have to learn to Bash and Block when fighting in this game which makes for a truly fun combat, more than any other RPG/MMO.  It is not just a hack and slash / cast spells  / shoot arrows, etc. You also have to block and bash at times.  Crafting is fun and challenging.  I make in game money selling crafted items at the guild store of 5 guilds I joined.  I haven't PVPed in a long  now and I am having so much fun just adventuring and crafting.  I have two steeds that I fed to max abilities, one for speed (race horse)and the other for bag space (pack horse).  You can also feed your horse for stamina.  There are so much more things to say but this is all for now.  When you see a bad review, check the date of the review because like I said, the bugs and always being fixed and bots I have not seen lately.    *From what I've read about some negative reviews is that some people complained that this game costs money, and you have to pay more for game subscription fees (this is the same for other popular MMO games and is normal for high quality online RPG/MMO)  Also unless you have played this game up to at least level 15, where you will be able to switch ready weapon sets / combat abilities with a touch of a button in the middle of combat (PvP or PvE), you haven't really experienced your true combat potential.*    I purchased two of the DIGITAL versions, one Imperial Edition for myself and one regular for my wife.  Having said that, my review is about the game and not the physical.    The beauty is in the details!  Even though a lot of players are previous fans of \\"The Elder Scrolls\\" lore and series of games, I believe newcomers will have the most fun in the world of Nirn because the lore about The Elder Scrolls and all things in Tamriel will be new to them!  That means some serious adventuring and fun.  Playing tip:  If sometimes you need help in figuring things out in the game, there are so many websites dedicated to \\"The Elder Scrolls Online\\" with all the tips and tricks to make life in Tamriel easier.  But of course, you can always be a hard-core adventurer and figure out all things by yourself.    When you enter this game, it feels, sounds, and looks like you are really in their world.  The music mesmerizing and the graphics superb.  All computer game characters are voiced over.  You'll be surprised some of those voices are from popular people such as Kate Beckinsale, John Cleese, Bill Nighy, Alfred Molina, Lynda Carter, Michael Gambon, Malcolm McDowell, to name some, although this is not important when playing. I found out about this after I made level 10 and decided to click on links on the \\"The Elder Scrolls Online\\" website.    Adventuring seems endless and easy but oh so rewarding.  Combat is fun, fight your own style, and challenging, yet never boring as I change up my fighting sequences.  Crafting is also fun and rewarding.  Create your own weapons, armor, potions, food and drinks then use or sell for gold coins. You can also sell your services by improving other player's equipment.    IMHO, this game will allow anyone to play just to Craft, PVE, PVP, Quest, Buy and Sell, or any combination of, or do all even.  In addition you can join Guilds, play with your partner, friends, groups, or big battles, or you can always play solo whenever you want.  It is a complete game world that will definitely make you forget about this Earthen world while you are in their world.    This game is not something you play in a few days to complete.  This game is about you (your person(s)/character(s) living in the world of the Elder Scrolls) growing and adventuring for weeks and even months.  I will not compare this game to great games like WoW, Everquest, DAoC, etc.  But I will say this game is in it's own category... and that new category is better than all previous RPG/MMO games.  Like what most people have said \\"This game is the new game to beat.\\"    It costs money up front and every month but so far (based on how much fun my friends and I have been having) it is worth every penny.  If you do not enjoy reading books, horse riding, crafting, adventuring, questing, PvE, PvP, soloing, grouping, big battles, strategizing, RPG, or MMO, and any combination of, then this game is not for you.  I even enjoyed taking a break from adventuring by reading the books in the game and also fishing.  I just now have to figure out where to put some of my trophy fishes.  My in game horse named \\"Gryf\\" runs faster after I've fed him apples (he must be the best part of the 'Imperial Edition' in addition to the tresure maps, and the magic rings of Mara that works only when myself and my wife are playing at the same time).    PS:  The developers of this game already planned to add more to the game as time goes on, and this in my mind makes up for paying the monthly subscription fees.  One account allows you to create as many as 8 characters on the US server and also 8 more characters on the European server if you'd like. (I found a lot more people on the European server that loves to Role Play). To save on subscription, the cheapest plan is to pay for 180 days which equals to $12.99 per month instead of the monthly payment plan of $14.99.($13.99/month for 90 days)

product_title: War of the Roses Kingmaker [Online Game Code]
review_body: I've logged a lot of time with this game and at first I was really impressed. Beware there is a steep learning curve. It's not that bad if you've played games like Mount & Blade: Warband though. This game has great gameplay and the premise is top-notch. The problems stem from the developer making it free-to-play long after it's release. It's scared away a lot of the veterans because of a variety of problems. Firstly, there are tons of laggers in this game. It's not their fault most of the time because there just aren't enough servers available to international players. They end up joining US servers and essentially ruin many battles. It's very frustrating to lose a duel based on someone's connection (most servers don't have ping limits). The other problem is hacking is quite prevalent. Most hackers use a cheat engine to just speed up their play, which isn't too obvious to everyone unless they speed it up to an excessive amount. This completely ruins the balance of the game because there are plenty of penalties on heavy armor, heavier weapons, missed swings, etc. that can be avoided by speed hackers. This wouldn't be too much of a problem except for the fact that people who hack often never get banned. I've seen people with names that brag about hacking and these guys are often high levels. You can report them through Steam which I have done multiple times and I still see those same players later on. Even if they were to get banned they can just create another account and start over (free-to-play). The developers of this game failed to address these facts and have moved on to promoting a new game (War of the Viking) which is essentially the same game with a few tweaks. I cannot recommend this game even though it has been very fun at times. I hope the devs figure this stuff out in their future endeavors.

product_title: Silent Hunter V: Battle of the Atlantic
review_body:
I have avoided buying this game up until now (it was deeply discounted) and I should have continued avoiding buying it. What a shame, i LOVED the silent hunter series up until this one.

First of all, you are required to sign up for ubisoft's \\"Upay\\" game network (which really just boils down to a chance to shove ads in your face). Thankfully, since this is a download version, you wont be stuck with their suc-u-rom shennanigans, but you will be forced to keep your save games on their servers for some unknown reason. Oh yea, i know the reason, Ubisoft sucks.

Next, they've tried to make the game more mouse-centered, which would be fine except they've botched the games mouse inputs, there is a distinct lag between inputs & results... even on a machine that has more than double the games system requirements.

Next, they've forced you to walk around the sub & click on stuff in order to get to the functions of the ship. Which would've been a good idea if they hadn't botched that up so horribly as well.

If only they would've just done a graphics improvement to SH4 & shoved that out the door... it would've been 10X the game that this is.

My advice is keep on waiting until its even cheaper than $10... or until someone (hopefully not ubisoft) releases SH6.

--edit-- Interesting side note... it seems that updating games is not something that upay does. Also odd that the game itself doesnt check for updates (odd since it saves your games on the internet, but cant check its own version number?) Also odd that the download & buy version doesnt include a patch that is now over 3 years old.

Anyway, long story short, this download gives you version 1.05.. in order to update it to 1.2 (which you WILL want to do) you'll have to go to C:\Ubisoft\Silent Hunter 5\Support\GameUpdater\ and run GU.exe

If i were a game maker, i'd have done it differently, but apparently thats the way ubi rolls.

This game has serious flaws that make it difficult for me to enjoy.
First: Simcity does not provide adequate information on how gameplay works. The simulation is complex, and it's not clear to the player what he should do to accomplish certain things. The included game manual provides very little information, and some of the messages in game are very misleading.
Second: Several gameplay mechanics are not working as expected. This may be due to the lack of documentation leading to the "wrong" expectations, but there are very intuitive expectations that the game violates. In some situations, the game shows data that is clearly self-contradicting.
Third: There is no acknowledgement of bugs. Therefore, it is not known whether any unexpected game behavior will change in a future patch or is an intentional gameplay element.

Be careful with buying additional content for this game. Simcity allows you to transfer ownership of your cities to other players. review_headline: I wanted very much to like this game
review_body:
I have been a might and magic fan since Might and Magic 6. After that I played Heroes of Might and Magic 2+ and consider these some of the best games ever created and by far the best replay ability of any fantasy games. Might and Magic X actually goes back to the age Might and Magic 5 in terms of game play and is very much unlike Might and Magic 6-9.
1) Both the adventure world and dungeons are turn based. You can move in north south east or west directions but not diagonally. It adds some tactical benefits to the game but feels hugely restrictive. It often happens that you get temporarily stuck on rocks, trees, etc because they stand in the way of your grid movement. As well, there are many times when walking around a curve you have to walk right walk forward walk right over and over again to make this movement happen. The landscapes have moved from the open large landscapes of MM6-9 to the smaller more enclosed landscapes that most games have today. Sure, there are trees and there are hills and there are landscape objects, but there is really only one small path you can travel through this area, the rest is just decoration for viewing and adds nothing more to the game. Unlike MM 6-9, you can no longer kite enemies or engage them from long distances. You simply walk into their preset aggressive range and you are locked in battle until one of you dies.
2) Monsters and dungeons of your level are grouped in same area together with high level monsters and dungeons. Having played the previous games, I understand that you can chose to go to an area that is too high for you and get handed your lunch by those higher level monsters- I have no problem with that. In fact that was part of the fun of the previous games is gathering buffs and weapons by risking a run through dangerous territory. In MMX, however, you will fight a monster right outside of the starting town and beat it. You will go to the next one, beat it, and then rest up to fully restore you health (camp). You then attack the third monster in that area and in two hits your entire group is dead. No warning, no indication of the monsters high level, and no way to retreat or run away once he engages you. You will find yourself saving the game after every encounter because of this bazaar randomness in monster placement. This happens all the time and you must expect to die a lot, not because you did anything wrong but because of the weird nature of this game.
3) I have quite a lot of money on me and would like to check another town for better equipment or spells. I found the road to the next town but it is blocked by a guard you cant attack or get by for any reason. I go back to the ship in the harbor but no ships are leaving the harbor. Stables? Nope. There is literately no way to get out of this town until certain quests have been completed. This makes the world feel very restrictive and linear just like the landscape.
4) Quests really give you very few cues how to complete them or what needs to be done. I went into one cave and it was a series of 6 plates on the floor. I stepped on them for a while and then looked it up on Google. There was a Youtube video showing what order to activate the plates it would require some 10+ steps, in precise order to do it. I found it so difficult to follow, even with the video, that I left the area and went on. You get quests in the first area that can't be completed until you get into other areas but the game does not tell you this. IE. I am getting quests that I want to do but I can't even physically get to that area yet because its blocked by impassible guards.
5) The games monster tactics can be summed up as follows. You see a monster ahead. You move ahead a few grid spaces to position yourself so that you have the advantage on the monster a bit. You make your move. Out of literally nowhere, monsters pop out of thin air behind and to both sides of you. This completely negates any advantage the game might get from grid based movement. Imagine Heroes of Might and Magic 3 in battle combat mode. You are level 5 (beginning of the game). You enter combat with an enemy hero with 3 monsters in his army - a sure win. The battle terrain spawns and grid based battle begins. However, instead of you starting on your side and him on his side, you are now in the middle surrounded by enemies on every side and his 3 monsters is now 20. This happens almost every fight in MMX and because of it, you should not even have a grid based map or movement because it is impossible to use it to tactical advantage when monsters pop out of thin air. In fact you might as well just have a button you click that spawns a room with random monsters in random positions to fight -similar to the Arena in Might and Magic 6. Even the combat in the MM6 Arena is better that combat in MMX because you could move around and avoid certain monsters while isolating others etc. You get none of that in MMX because once you and a moster are right next to each other you can't move at all in any direction even if you have done nothing that turn.
6) Graphics. I have read a LOT of reviews that complained about the graphics. For me, I actually think the graphics are good but nothing to rave about. They do not detract from the game at all in my opinion. What does detract from the game, as mention before, is the restrictive feel of the landscapes. Sure there is a huge forest here but only a few tiny paths can be walked on by your character. Many times, that path is only one grid space wide with a few branches that dead end a short way off the path. One grid space is equal to the area that your party is standing on any any time so you follow this tiny path just big enough to fit your party through a huge forest of window dressing that has absolutely no meaning in the game. You cant interact with it in any way including walking through it.
7) The user interface is pretty well done in my opinion. Spell placement and ease of use is very good as are the inventory, spell book, stats and skills screens. Sound and music is good.
8) Uplay sucks of course because now every game company is going to have a service similar to Steam. I understand the value of this for the company but for the user what happens when that company goes belly up because of some stupid decision a CEO made. Who is going to maintain the Uplay service no to mention 10 more username / password accounts that you have to keep track of for game companies.
Overall I am disappointed with this game and believe it is a step backward in terms of the Might and Magic series. review_headline: FTL: Learning how to play the hand delt to you
review_body:
FTL can be considered a game of many genre's, but I prefer to think of it as game of chance. I will get into what I mean by this later, but needless to say if you HATE games that take some of the control on winning or losing from you, don't purchase this game.

A quick description of the game would be: You are a ship trying to go from one end of the galaxy to the other to deliever a report on a Genocidal enemy fleet. Exploring planets and bases in each Solar system as you move forward can lead to fights or random encounters, which can be a blessing or a curse, pending your supplies and health. You can only explore each solar system for so long, as a massive enemy fleet that will destroy you in moments arrives in each solar system you jump to, to kill you. As you travel, you can gain new crew members, from different species that can drastically change your ships survivability. As you progress, the threat of death at your heels, and unknown doom every planet you explore, makes for one of the most exciting games you could ever play.

FTL has to be one of the most enjoyable games I have played in years. Even when dying, you learn so much in each game, that you are happy to hit new game and start again. Rarely did I get frustrated with the game, even when it seemed stacked against me, because there are so many incentives the game gives you to replay. You don't have to beat the game to unlock new ships, or races to play as; you only have to obtain achievements for new content. Simply, you don't have to reach the end to have a new experience with the game. While nothing else carries over (money and such) the games system allows you to never feel like it was all for naught, and is a driving point for me to keep playing.
The battle system is fun, with multiple tactics to employe, you can either bludgeon the ships health to death with superior firepower, fight conservatively knowing where to hit, keeping them in a constant state of panic as their crewdies from a variety of ways, or board the enemy ship and slaughter the crew one on one. Even the most unfair seeming fights can be won when interchanging your tactics, making the reward so much sweeter as you beat a vastly superior ship.
The open space, the random encounters, can be overwhelming, or haunting at times. It always seems like you discover one more thing, or face an encounter in a brand new way because of one miniscule variable that changes the game drastically. The general ambiance is just amazing, with mystery, fear, and uncertainty gripping your attention.

What I opened with about FTL being a gambling game more than anything else, is that the games random generation of events can make the game feel like it personally hates you. To begin, you can get stuck fighting battle after battle, with nothing to heal you until you hit the end of a solar system. While you might find this frustrating your first few games (if you are getting unlucky) it always makes me want to play one more game. Its like playing slots or blackjack, you know you are just a game away from a giant payout. The involvement that FTL makes you take with each new game, makes the excitement restart every time, one that I can't get from any other game when replaying it. Suffice to say, purchase FTL, unless the idea of getting screwed by the hand dealt to you is unbearable, you won't regret it.

product_title: Batman: Arkham Asylum Game of the Year Edition
review_body:
If you played through the old 8-bit and 16-bit days and even into the DVD based systems, you know just how bad Batman games were. They were right on par with Spider-man games which were mostly frustrating, weird, and didn't feel like you were playing as the hero you saw on TV or in the comics. We've come a long way.

The Joker has allowed himself to be captured and taken to Arkham. No sooner is he in than he springs his trap and away we go. The game world is nicely detailed and things look realistic without having to have a $200 graphics card. I'm running a GT 240 I got around 3 years ago and everything runs smooth as silk.

You have access to gadgets like explosive jell, your baterrangs, and grappling hook. You also have a very cool "Detective Mode" which lets you see through walls via infrared and helps point out walls you can blow up. It also shows you the state of enemies (calm/tense/terrified) and picks out thugs with firearms. Combat is fun. Controls streamlined. Everything is polished. It manages to take care of almost every major complaint one has about a game being unfun.

The only thing I'd say against it, all the streamlining makes some of the moves feel like autopilot. At times it felt more like I was just pressing buttons to watch a movie than playing a game. It can also be a little hint happy and feel like it's just telling you where to go next. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, one of my major annoyances is if I get lost in a game and waste time not doing anything fun, but it'd have been a little better if it waited to see you were lost and then started getting progressively more "helpful" in the hints. All told though, spectacular game.

Graphics are good, and it runs fine on my mid-range DX11 intel core i5 laptop w/ 4GB RAM, Geforce GT420M 1GB video card. I can't run full settings, but it still looks good.

review_headline: Not New, Not Hardcore, Not Particularly Remarkable
review_body:
I bought this game to circumvent the Steam Greenlight process, which takes approximately 7 eons. The Greenlight page for Cook, Serve, Delicious claims that it \\"is a hardcore restaurant sim, one of the few in its genre that gives the players total control over where they want to take their restaurant.\\" This, along with some other text I read about how the developers felt there was not enough hardcore restaurant sims out there, gave me hope.

I was hoping for something like Crusader Kings, but with restaurants: spreadsheets and statistics, a game where you can take your restaurant in any number of directions.

This is not that game.

This is an almost bog-standard cooking/restaurant/speed game, where customers file into your restaurant in dribs, drabs, or torrents, and where you are solely responsible for serving them a menu (customizable, but only from 18-20 prototypes). These customers have little patience for sloth, and less for mistakes: one spritz of spice too few or chicken breast tenderized too much will ruin their expectations. The gameplay consists of a manic attempt to balance different recipes, which cook at different speeds and require a different set of keystrokes to enter. You are paid, if the customers are not too unhappy with you. You can spend this pittance on a few kitchen upgrades, a few patience upgrades, and a few recipe upgrades (which make the recipes more complicated to prepare, but also more expensive).

There are a few flashes of innovation: I enjoyed the email system, and some of the graphics (particularly the skyline through the window) are quite lovely. The game has a sense of humor, and is pretty cohesive. It's an enjoyable way to occupy my hands while I think about other things.

But it is padded; I have no doubt that it will indeed take me the 30 hours listed to finish the game because the developers have instituted time requirements for each level: 20 days per star, 5 stars total. There are other requirements (relatively easy to fulfill) that I usually have completed in half that time, meaning that there are about half the time is pure grind. Because you don't earn enough per day to buy something new every day, that grind time is *really* grindy, and one of the things that I'm least happy about. There are already other barriers to game pacing in place that work fine (money you can earn, limits on your speed/coordination, etc.) It is completely unnecessary to force players to sit longer before accessing content. It's borderline marketing dishonesty to claim this is part of gameplay hours; if there's 30 hours of gameplay *only* because the developers set an egg timer to prevent you from accessing content, that's pretty shody design and ethics.

There's basically one path: if you want to sell hamburgers and fries, you can, but you don't have any decor options, and the restaurant doesn't *feel* any different. It's clear from the goals you're given that the designers want you to claw your way to the top (indeed, it's unavoidable). At some point, several of the foods can't be served any more - if you wanted to run a little snack bar, you're out of luck within a few hours of gameplay.

The game appears to have gone through pretty thorough quality assurance and editing, and I appreciate that. It's a fine game, for what it is, but you should not go in expecting anything more than a polished dash-sim.

review_headline: Got this game for free and I still feel ripped off.
review_body:
I got this free with my new video card, so I guess I should be grateful for because if I paid money for this I'd be raging right now. Where to begin?

The story - Can't say much about the story since I got bored to death and stopped paying attention. It's not that the story itself is boring, but the way it is presented. Everything is done incredibly sllloooooowwwwwwwwwlllyyyy. Characters narrate for what seems like forever speaking like robots. Either you are forced to sit there with no control and listen to them drone on, or (even worse) follow them as they incredibly slowly walk while giving exposition. They scripted so much in this game, why not that? Also I lost track as to why I am chasing the Dark One instead of not contacting home base to let them know of army heading their way. You'd think that would be slightly more important. Also get use to being captured. It's now your hobby.

No control - Around the first hour or so the computer is playing the game, not you. It's all one long escort quest with you following someone else, and we all know how much fun that is. And most of the fights during that hour are also scripted, so fighting back feels pointless and a waste of ammo since it's programed so you either can't win or can't lose.

AI - I haven't seen AI this bad in literally decades. Just wait around a corner and enemies will slowly come around the bend to get a bullet in the head, oblivious to the pile of bodies of his friends that just did the same thing. The game promotes stealth, but they are so stupid you can just walk into a room and start shooting and kill everyone before they react. Literally you can stand behind one enemy and shoot one on the other side of the room and the one right in front of you will just stand there for 5 seconds saying \\"Huh? What was that? Are you o.k.?\\" Also enemies will stand in the open and loudly proclaim that they are reloading. Brilliant survival strategy there!

I'm lost! - Thisone is small but important. There is no hud, directional arrow, journal or map to tell you where you going. I know this was left out to give a more realistic experience, but at least they could give you a journal to tell you your current objective. I died in the swamp because I couldn't remember the second place to look for gasoline. Normally I like a bit of exploring is fine, but not when I have a limited air supply. Also after one of my many captures I was stuck in one room for 15 minutes because I couldn't find the exit (see graphics below.)

Graphics - On the surface the graphics are great. The game looks very good, provided you like the color brown and from what you can see out of a blurry, broken gas mask (Note to designers: modern gas mask lenses are plastic, not glass!) What is hidden behind that shiny coat is held together with string and glue. Clipping thru objects is constant, as well as enemies hitting you thru walls. At times you'll want to explore a hallway but find it blocked by a table or the invincible small cardboard box. Creatures react when you shoot them...sometimes. Either that or they have a very weird hit box. If they swing and miss they will sometimes spaz out. The programmers spent a lot of time creating a 7 second scene of you getting in and out of the rail car, but then block your path with a small box. That right there sums up this game; massive amount of work went into pointless stuff and not main game elements. There is also a constant bug where the screen will lock up for around 30 seconds. I have not checked to see if there is a fix for that yet.

I could keep going, but that sums up most of the bad points. If the story grabbed me in the beginning I guess I might like this more. As it stands it is a slow, boring story broken up by brief sections of boring combat. I could stand one or the other being bad, but not both.

product_title: Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn
review_body:
First I'll let you know why I took off 1 star. I took it off because of how terrible the launch for this game has been ,while most MMO's do suffer from poor launches I feel like this one was a little more stressful.

Now for a review of the actual game.

Pros

- Beautiful graphics
- Extensive amount of content
- Unique dungeons
- Challenging boss fights
- Great story
- Side quests are interesting
- Able to level each class and job to level 50 on one toon.
- Large map you'll want to explore
- FATE's are fun

Cons

- Server errors (only at launch)
- Frustrating minimap
- Long grind after leveling first job.
- Combat is a little slow
- No PvP

I've been playing the game since Closed Beta 2 and experienced the game in it's and worst times. I did not however play 1.0 so you'll see no comparison from me but from what I've heard this is leagues better than 1.0.

Now what a lot of people are going to think when seeing this game is \\"Is this a WoW clone?\\". I can safely say that no, it is not. It does have a traditional MMORPG structure ala questing, dungeons, raids, and skills but besides that when you play this game it will feel like a fresh experience. After playing for over 50 hours since Open beta began I still haven't gotten burned out by this game and it just keeps getting more and more addicting. The amount of content pumped into this game is astounding and there's always something to do. You can primarily do quests and still be able to reach level 50, or you could simply run dungeons and get to level 50. You really have the option to play this game however you like.

Crafting in this game is one of the cool features in my opinion that sets it apart from other MMORPG's. You level up a job like fishing or alchemy the same you do a class. There's even job specific gear you get that provide stats that help with your job. Each job alsohas unique skills you learn as you level up.

Now for another question burning in people's minds, is it worth $15 a month? Short answer, yes. Like I said before the amount of content you get in this game is astounding and I feel like you can't go wrong paying the subscription fee. Unlike a Free to play game everything is available to you, no cash shops or anything that would give someone who pays more money an advantage over anyone else.

My final words on the game are this, if you're a Final Fantasy fan, MMORPG veteran or even a complete noob when it comes to video games you will love Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn. It is very fun and very addicting and I game that I can see being very successful in the future.

Remember games like Sonic the Hedgehog, TMNT, Kid Chameleon, or even Mario? Yeah, well we haven't seen a game like those in awhile (especially a 2D one) and that's what makes `Splosion Man so great. It brings back that classic challenging platformer goodness with a great sense of humor, and a loving character. `Splosion Man pits you against a bunch of mad scientists obstacles and traps trying to capture while you run rampant trying to escape.

As the name implies you have the ability to explode, but not just as many times as you want. You can explode three times in a row then you must \\"recharge\\" yourself by staying on the ground for a few seconds or clinging to a wall. Exploding allows you to jump, break glass, hit switches, and pretty much do anything because this is the core gameplay. You have different obstacles to overcome such as jumping gaps; you may need a green canister to shoot you across a huge gap, exploding barrels will give you a slight boost since there may be huge open areas above a death pit that are just barrels. The idea would be to explode yourself on each barrel and \\"hop\\" across the huge gap. Most of the time scientists will pull levers that block your way and you must solve how to get to them. Giant closing walls may come down on you from either side and you'll need to jump your way up and out. You may run across electrified fields, and you must find the switch to turn them off, then you can kill the scientist and be on your marry way. There are dozens of different traps and obstacles and it would take forever to describe them all, but one thing is for certain and it's that you need to use your exploding powers to get through them.

When it comes to boss fights they are epic and rather tough. They all involve some form of exploding and evading which must be mastered. That's the beauty of this game; you can conquer the controls, but it takes practice to master them. The later levels require precise jumping, exploding, and timing or you will meet your death. Speaking of death (unlike older platformers) checkpoints are fair and plentiful so you are sure not to get to frustrated. Trial and error here is abundant, but it's forgiving. What I mainly love about the character you play are the noises he makes. He runs around looking goofier than ever making airplane noises, barking noises, and just overall maniacal laughs that make you laugh every time. The achievements on the the other hand are pretty easy to get and take a bit of thinking to figure out. Most of them require finishing certain objectives and some require finding hidden items. Like any platformer the game has impossible to find items and these are cakes. Yes they even make a joke about the Portal reference in the achievement description. Hell, there's even a real life `Splosion Man video during the credits roll. Speaking of that the game has a great co-op play both online and off so you and a friend can master the power of exploding. You even unlock a theme and gamer picture for all your effort.

So to conclude, `Splosion Man is a fine platformer which does something original that we have never seen before. Whether it's the epic boss fights, the ability to explode, or the levels that just make you feel giddy `Splosion is worth every penny and will hopefully make an explosive sequel.'s the beauty of this game; you can conquer the controls, but it takes practice to master them. review_headline: Solid game that could use more content.
review_body: If you expected cerebral pleasures from a game called \\"Alien Shooter\\", you have the wrong game. If you want to reduce about 4,500--by my kill stats--ugly critters large and small to stacks of corpses and pools of gore, you're dead on.    AS2 is a simple 3rd-person shooter (TPS) with isometric presentation. ( [...] ) There's no strategy to the game; tactics are simple, and it has a very linear simplicity. You can occasionally make a few extra weapons and support items available by finding hidden/obscure objects, but nearly all hidden areas are simply stashes of cash and/or ammo; this means you're likely to live longer, and contributes directly to your final score no matter what. Cash goes directly to buying better weapons and support gear from a sort of futuristic storefront: one per level, with a few levels that don't make it available at all. You'll want to plan accordingly; death means restarting a level, no matter how long, from the beginning.    If difficulty becomes a problem, there are quite a lot of cheats packed in; many very granular. You *will* be labeled a cheater, and unable to upload your \\"high score\\", but at least you can be assured you'll finish the game. You can also edit game resources--that's outside the scope of this review.    The plot is forgivably bad, and exists to provide some minimal context to grinding a bloody path through the advancing alien hordes. There's voice acting: some passable, some laughable. The game-interface text is translated competently and even amusingly (see the description of the \\"Awareness\\" trait, or whatever it's called), whereas a good deal of the monologue / dialogue, mostly the written parts, seem to have been translated by the Russian developers using Google Language Tools. It's understandable, but not much better than that.    Yet, the mistranslations aren't game-stopping, and you've got your pick of around 120 unique weapons ranging up to \\"impossible, yet awesome\\" and 50 or so support items--if you count all the cybernetic implant variants. It's just what I need for turning my brain off once in a while.    --barely playable on a fast Core 2 Duo with Intel HD 3000 graphics. You'll want a real GPU for this one, if not a fast one.

product_title: Dark Souls: Prepare To Die Edition [Online Game Code]
review_body:
The core idea of Dark Souls isn't too bad. Difficult monsters and very little hand-holding. I'd play a game like that. The game has a few design problems I could live with, but what really cripples this game is how crappy a port it is.

The controls are terrible. Absolute trash. It's twin stick controls, so you don't move well. Turn speed is pretty slow. You have to lock on to someone to target them, but you can only lock on if you're pretty close. If you try to lock on but you're too far away, it moves the camera behind you. If the camera was in front of you, that turns you around. That's very very bad if you were trying to move away from something and lock onto it, because now you've moving towards it (and still not locked on).

The on-screen prompts are all xbox buttons, so if you don't have an xbox controller, you are out of luck. Don't try playing with mouse+keyboard, because you will need at least 3 hands.

If you have another kind of gamepad, you're stuck with whatever autoconfigured controls it assigns. For me several buttons were swapped, which is weird. Not that I'd know they were wrong, since again all the prompts are xbox.

So the controls are pretty objectively bad, but there are a few subjective things I really dislike.

You'll probably end up spending more time redoing content than anything else. What happens to me is I'll have a first run through someplace and it'll be kind of fun. Exploration, edge of my seat tension, and so on. Then I'll die somewhere, so everything respawns. Great. Now I have to repeat the last hour's worth of content. It's not as fun because I've already seen it, but whatever. Then I die again, so that's another run through this stuff. Repeat enough times and it's just boring and frustrating. If you play sloppy or try to run past things, you'll probably just die more.

It's possible to grind out xp indefinitely to raise your stats very high. That means ifI wanted to spent 8 hours leveling I could wear better armor. But I don't want to grind because grinding is boring, so I'm at a disadvantage. Some people like that sort of thing, but I think it's pretty bad.

The magic system is kind of stupid. It's spells per day, and it sucks as much as it does in D&D. Buy spells from vendors (if you can find them), raise a stat to equip them. Non-casters don't have per-day limitations, but I guess they couldn't be bothered to come up with a more interesting, less awful system for spells.

So in summary: It's a so-so opaque rpg with lots of deadly monsters, but it's ruined by awful controls and mandatory content repetition. The spell system stinks, too.

product_title: Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Standard Edition [Download]
review_headline: Says it is a game, but feels like a visionary tale!
review_body:
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is the most engrossing game I have played since the original Mass Effect and Dragon Age Origins. I may draw flak for this, but I enjoyed it even more than the original Deus Ex. Deus Ex: Human Revolution manages to suck the player into the game world in a way that makes other developers appear lazy. I felt for many of the characters, especially the lead character and the tragedy in his life, even finding it very interesting that he was interested in renascence era clockworks (he has been building them in his apartment from blueprints). There is a bit of a let down as we don't get quite the closure with some of the characters near the end that would have been hoped for as becoming humanity's savior takes precedence.

You play as Adam Jensen, the head of security for an up and coming trans-human augment corporation. Unfortunately, Adam's life is turned upside down when an attack nearly kills him, leading to him to need life saving augmentations throughout his body. Jensen takes a sabbatical from work to adjust to his situation; however, events cause Jensen to need to return to work six months after the incident. The plot keeps you motivated and has a lot of twists and turns. Without any DLC and playing as a mix of ninja, hacker, and gunslinger, I clocked 35 hours from start to finish of a single play through. There are so many fun ways to approach any given section, you might be able to cloak and completely sneak by, move from object to object and knock out a few guards along the way, hack a gun turret or robots to obliterate the enemies in a room, punch through a wall and start blasting away with a minigun, set up some traps, or even completely avoid an area by jumping a fence or slipping into an airduct. There is no excuse to not enjoy the game because you can literally play it any way you want.

The only real weak point of the game is that boss fights can be a little bit rough on normal difficulty levels if you don't prepare for them with at least a few combat augmentations found on the Dermal Armor line (especially EMP shielding). The first boss was a bit tough for me, the second took a moderate amount of trial and error; however, by the third, I had enough augmentations across the board to take him down after only a couple of tries. The final boss was a complete push over for me as I could hack anything with an interface while laughing off most gunfire and EMP blasts, and had upgraded my revolver while stockpiling ammo for it to a point that would make Dirty Harry green with envy. Having mentioned stockpiling ammo, soldiers in the future seem to be able to pop off hundreds of rounds when they spot you while only ever carrying 2 or 3 rounds for you to take from their person; likewise, someone missed the memo that ammo usually comes 50 rounds to a box! You'll need to scrounge a lot of ammo and be proficient in several weapons to make it through the game if you are aren't planning a 100% sneaky approach (I carried both pistols, a tranquilizer rifle, a minigun, a stun gun, and an assault rifle for most of the game and used whichever had ammo on hand or best dealt with the situation).

Ultimately, not only will you enjoy this game, but it will make you think. I found myself asking a lot of questions about the ethics of transhumanism and what makes us indeed human. More developers need to be willing to explore and interweave issues like this into their storytelling. This game is money well spent; however, you may want to get the augmented edition for the extras like the soundtrack (the musical score by the way is superb, as is the acting and art direction). What are you waiting for? Add to cart!

Quantum Conundrum, a game by Kim Swift. Kim Swift was a part of making Portal and it shows through in some aspects of the game. In Quantum Conundrum you are a young boy sent to your uncle's house who happens to be a crazy scientist. When you arrive there doesn't seem to be anyone home. Then you hear your uncle start to talk to you through some communication device and he seems to be stuck in some other dimension. He guides you through these different rooms with one puzzle in each, much like oh I don't know test chambers from Portal. After a short tutorial you are given the Inter-Dimensional Shift Device.
This is when you start to have control over what dimension you're in there are 5 total including the regular dimension. The first dimension you get is the fluffy dimension which makes everything all pink and fluffy, but it also makes thinks lighter like a safe so you can pick it up. Each dimension has its own slightly different art styles which is nice because the whole game looks exactly the same. The second dimension you get is the heavy dimension which explains itself, and I won't get into the other 2. When you do in fact have all the dimensions at once it makes for some devilish puzzles.
To be upfront the game is pretty good with that said i find myself getting the answer to a puzzle and just not being able to execute it because i missed some jump or i didn't catch that thing in time and holy shit that is one of the most frustrating things when you mind know what to do but you just can't get it to work just right in the game. First person platforming is just no fun because you mess it up so much or at least i do. The game is way too focused on platforming, tight timing, and catching shit.
Now on to the part where I talk about the writing in the game. It's nowhere near that of Portal's. It kind of feels like it was written for a little kid. Which I guess makes since because the main character is a little kid, but even then they could have throughin some weird references to more adult things. It just sort of feels bland at some point. There's not even really that much of a story your uncles lost in some other dimension and it's your job to go find him. Whole game is cut with him saying stuff which is spouse to be funny, but it's not and he seemed to be talking about 90 percent of the time I was playing.
Quantum Conundrum is not bad in any since of the word, but it defiantly has its fair share of problems. The story and writing could use some work as well as just the overall design aspect of a lot of the puzzles. It does bring a lot of neat ideas to the table witch are always fun to play around with. For 15 bucks the game actually felt pretty long it was at least 7 hours for me personally, and I had a pretty good time with it.

Another compliant (a minor one) is that there is no entry in the Help section to explain the function of the feather and magnet and other special tiles. If I don't play the game for a few weeks, I may forget how to use the tiles. Going to the help section is not illuminating.

Lastly, it would be nice if there was an option to show all the matches for a particular tile. Again (and this goes beyond matches of flowers or seasons, etc), it can be difficult to figure out which tiles are matches while not being exact matches (if that makes any sense).There can be a penalty for this (a few pearls), but again in a game where you are scored on how quickly the set is cleared away, this would be a boon.

All that said, though, it is an enjoyable game and a great time waster.
